children: Popeyes is hoping yet another fried chicken sandwich can help revive its struggling business. To the rescue: a couple of packs of sweet honey sauce and a big biscuit.

The fried-chicken chain-with roughly $7.8 billion global sales and nearly 5,500 locations worldwide-introduced its Honey Chicken Biscuit nationwide on Monday priced at $5. (Prices vary by location!) The sandwich combines Popeye's signature chicken fillet with an enlarged buttermilk biscuit and the honey sauce.

Popeyes said the product was inspired by customers who have long experimented with combining its chicken, biscuits and honey. Chief Marketing Officer Matt Rubin described the sandwich as a way of turning familiar ingredients into something new.

The launch recalls Popeyes' original chicken sandwich, which became a viral sensation in August 2019 and sold out nationwide in roughly two weeks. The sandwich returned that November as a permanent menu item and helped generate extraordinary sales growth.

At the time, management explicitly credited the sandwich for the surge. Popeyes' U.S. comparable sales jumped 10.2% in the third quarter of 2019 before accelerating to 37.9% in the fourth quarter. Then-CEO Jose Cil called the product a game changer for the brand.

The momentum proved more than a passing fad: U.S. comparable sales rose nearly 30% in the first and second quarter of 2020 despite the Covid-19 pandemic. By early 2021, annual sales per restaurant had surpassed $1.8 million, up from $1.4 million before the sandwich's debut.

Seven years later, Popeyes could use another hit. Its U.S. comparable sales declined 5.2% in the second quarter of 2026. Systemwide sales in the U.S. and Canada fell 3.1% to $1.53 billion, while adjusted operating income dropped to $63 million from $66 million a year earlier.

The chain's struggles goes beyond weak consumer spending. At its February investor day, Popeyes executives said the chain had become overly reliant on limited-time promotions, which attracted new customers but failed to generate repeat visits.

The constant introduction of new products also complicated restaurant operations, contributing to inconsistent service, management said, while marketing drifted away from the chain's core offerings and Louisiana heritage amid intensifying competition in the fast-food chicken category.

Popeyes has since refocused on its signature chicken, tenders and sandwiches, expanded employee training, and introduced value offerings. Management said those initiatives were helping stabilize traffic and expected positive comparable sales in the second half of 2026.

Despite Popeyes' struggles, its parent company, Restaurant Brands, has continued to deliver solid growth, buoyed by stronger performance at its other chains. Global comparable sales increased 3.8% in the second quarter, fueled by an 8.5% growth at Burger King's U.S. business and 5.5% growth across international markets.

Adjusted earnings per share rose nearly 13% from a year earlier, although Tim Hortons, the company's largest earnings contributor, has also shown signs of slowing growth. Restaurant Brands expects to see an 8% growth in organic adjusted operating income for the full year.

Popeyes' North American operations accounted for just 12% of the company's global systemwide sales in the second quarter, compared with 25% from Burger King in the U.S. and Canada, 16% from Tim Hortons, and 44% from its international division.

That means even a hypothetical 10% increase in Popeyes' North American sales would add only about 1.2% to Restaurant Brands' systemwide sales. And because most Popeyes restaurants are franchised, only a fraction of the additional sales would flow to the parent company's top line through royalties and other franchise-related revenue.

A successful launch of the Honey Chicken Biscuit could nevertheless help Popeyes rebuild customer traffic. The challenge isn't getting customers to try another chicken sandwich. It's giving them a reason to come back.
